tagline: Chile's 'Jewel of the Pacific' climbs 45 hills in a riot of painted houses, rickety funiculars and some of the best street art in South America.
overview: Before the Panama Canal, Valparaíso was the busiest port on South America's Pacific coast. Sailors from everywhere left their mark — colourful zinc-clad houses stacked on 45 hills, historic funicular elevators called ascensores, and a bohemian culture that persists.

The city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and an open-air gallery: murals cover staircases, walls and houses across Cerro Alegre and Cerro Concepción, the two postcard hills of cafés, viewpoints and little museums. La Sebastiana, Pablo Neruda's quirky hilltop house-museum, looks over the bay.

Valpo keeps a working port's grit beneath the paint — fish markets, sailors' bars, harbour tours — and its New Year's Eve fireworks over the bay are the biggest in South America. Neighbouring Viña del Mar supplies the beaches.

funFacts.title: THE OLDEST FUNICULARS
funFacts.text: Ascensores — hillside elevators — have carried residents uphill since 1883.

funFacts.text: Pablo Neruda's five-storey hideaway La Sebastiana is now a museum of his collections.

funFacts.title: STREET ART CAPITAL

funFacts.text: Before the Panama Canal opened in 1914, ships rounding the Horn made Valpo rich.

funFacts.title: THE JEWEL OF THE PACIFIC
funFacts.text: Chileans call it 'Valpo' — and Pablo Neruda wrote odes to it.

funFacts.title: GRAFFITI ON EVERYTHING

funFacts.title: ASCENSOR LEGACY
